# wasm_bindgen_backend - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen-backend/

## Expand description

A common backend for bindgen crates.

This (internal) crate provides functionality common to multiple bindgen dependency crates. There are 4 main things exported from this crate:

-
Provides the ability to attempt conversion from an AST struct into a TokenStream
-
A struct used to provide diagnostic responses for failures of said tokenization
-
Abstract Syntax Tree types used to represent a Rust program, with the necessary metadata to generate bindings for it
-
Common utilities for manipulating parsed types from syn

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [ast](https://docs.rs/ast/index.html)
- A representation of the Abstract Syntax Tree of a Rust program, with all the added metadata necessary to generate Wasm bindings for it.
- [util](https://docs.rs/util/index.html)
- Common utility function for manipulating syn types and handling parsed values

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [bail_](https://docs.rs/macro.bail_span.html)- span
- Immediately fail and return an Err, with the arguments passed to err_span!
- [err_](https://docs.rs/macro.err_span.html)- span
- Provide a Diagnostic with the given span and message

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Diagnostic](https://docs.rs/struct.Diagnostic.html)
- A struct representing a diagnostic to emit to the end-user as an error.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [TryTo](https://docs.rs/trait.TryToTokens.html)- Tokens
- A trait for converting AST structs into Tokens and adding them to a TokenStream, or providing a diagnostic if conversion fails.

---

# bumpalo - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bumpalo/^3.0.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#bumpalo)`bumpalo`

**A fast bump allocation arena for Rust.**

[§](https://docs.rs#bump-allocation)Bump Allocation

Bump allocation is a fast, but limited approach to allocation. We have a chunk
of memory, and we maintain a pointer within that memory. Whenever we allocate an
object, we do a quick check that we have enough capacity left in our chunk to
allocate the object and then update the pointer by the object’s size. *That’s
it!*

The disadvantage of bump allocation is that there is no general way to deallocate individual objects or reclaim the memory region for a no-longer-in-use object.

These trade offs make bump allocation well-suited for *phase-oriented*
allocations. That is, a group of objects that will all be allocated during the
same program phase, used, and then can all be deallocated together as a group.

[§](https://docs.rs#deallocation-en-masse-but-no-drop)Deallocation en Masse, but no `Drop`

To deallocate all the objects in the arena at once, we can simply reset the bump
pointer back to the start of the arena’s memory chunk. This makes mass
deallocation *extremely* fast, but allocated objects’ [ Drop](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ops/trait.Drop.html) implementations are
not invoked.

However:[can be used to wrap](https://docs.rs/bumpalo/latest/bumpalo/boxed/struct.Box.html)`bumpalo::boxed::Box<T>``T`values allocated in the`Bump`arena, and calls`T`’s`Drop`implementation when the`Box<T>`wrapper goes out of scope. This is similar to how[works, except without deallocating its backing memory.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/boxed/struct.Box.html)`std::boxed::Box`

[§](https://docs.rs#what-happens-when-the-memory-chunk-is-full)What happens when the memory chunk is full?

This implementation will allocate a new memory chunk from the global allocator and then start bump allocating into this new memory chunk.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use bumpalo::Bump;
struct Doggo {
    cuteness: u64,
    age: u8,
    scritches_required: bool,
}
// Create a new arena to bump allocate into.
let bump = Bump::new();
// Allocate values into the arena.
let scooter = bump.alloc(Doggo {
    cuteness: u64::MAX,
    age: 8,
    scritches_required: true,
});
// Exclusive, mutable references to the just-allocated value are returned.
assert!(scooter.scritches_required);
scooter.age += 1;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#collections)Collections

When the `"collections"` cargo feature is enabled, a fork of some of the `std`
library’s collections are available in the [ collections](https://docs.rs/bumpalo/latest/bumpalo/collections/index.html) module. These
collection types are modified to allocate their space inside

`bumpalo::Bump`
arenas.```
#[cfg(feature = "collections")]
{
    use bumpalo::{Bump, collections::Vec};
    // Create a new bump arena.
    let bump = Bump::new();
    // Create a vector of integers whose storage is backed by the bump arena. The
    // vector cannot outlive its backing arena, and this property is enforced with
    // Rust's lifetime rules.
    let mut v = Vec::new_in(&bump);
    // Push a bunch of integers onto `v`!
    for i in 0..100 {
        v.push(i);
    }
}
```
Eventually [all  std collection types will be parameterized by an
allocator](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/42774) and we can remove
this

`collections` module and use the `std` versions.For unstable, nightly-only support for custom allocators in `std`, see the
`allocator_api` section below.

[§](https://docs.rs#bumpaloboxedbox)`bumpalo::boxed::Box`

When the `"boxed"` cargo feature is enabled, a fork of `std::boxed::Box`
is available in the `boxed` module. This `Box` type is modified to allocate its
space inside `bumpalo::Bump` arenas.

**A  Box<T> runs T’s drop implementation when the Box<T> is dropped.** You
can use this to work around the fact that

`Bump` does not drop values allocated
in its space itself.```
#[cfg(feature = "boxed")]
{
    use bumpalo::{Bump, boxed::Box};
    use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering};
    static NUM_DROPPED: AtomicUsize = AtomicUsize::new(0);
    struct CountDrops;
    impl Drop for CountDrops {
        fn drop(&mut self) {
            NUM_DROPPED.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
        }
    }
    // Create a new bump arena.
    let bump = Bump::new();
    // Create a `CountDrops` inside the bump arena.
    let mut c = Box::new_in(CountDrops, &bump);
    // No `CountDrops` have been dropped yet.
    assert_eq!(NUM_DROPPED.load(Ordering::SeqCst), 0);
    // Drop our `Box<CountDrops>`.
    drop(c);
    // Its `Drop` implementation was run, and so `NUM_DROPS` has been
    // incremented.
    assert_eq!(NUM_DROPPED.load(Ordering::SeqCst), 1);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Adding the `serde` feature flag will enable transparent serialization of `Vec`s, `String`s
and boxed values.

```
[dependencies]
bumpalo = { version = "3.18", features = ["collections", "boxed", "serde"] }
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use bumpalo::{Bump, boxed::Box, collections::Vec};
// Create a new bump arena.
let bump = Bump::new();
// Create a `Box`
let box = Box::new_in("hello", &bump);
// Serialize with serde_json
assert_eq!(serde_json::to_string(&box).unwrap(), "\"hello\"");
// Create a `Vec`
let vec = Vec::new_in( &bump);
vec.push(1);
vec.push(2);
// Serialize with serde_json
assert_eq!(serde_json::to_string(&vec).unwrap(), "[1, 2]");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#no_std-support)`#![no_std]` Support

Bumpalo is a `no_std` crate by default. It depends only on the `alloc` and `core` crates.

[§](https://docs.rs#std-support)`std` Support

You can optionally decide to enable the `std` feature in order to enable some
std only trait implementations for some collections:

- `std::io::Write`for- `Vec<'bump, u8>`

[§](https://docs.rs#thread-support)Thread support

The `Bump` is `!Sync`, which makes it hard to use in certain situations around
threads ‒ for example in `rayon`.

The [ bumpalo-herd](https://crates.io/crates/bumpalo-herd) crate provides a
pool of

`Bump` allocators for use in such situations.[§](https://docs.rs#nightly-rust-allocator_api-support)Nightly Rust `allocator_api` Support

The unstable, nightly-only Rust `allocator_api` feature defines an [ Allocator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/alloc/trait.Allocator.html)
trait and exposes custom allocators for

`std` types. Bumpalo has a matching
`allocator_api` cargo feature to enable implementing `Allocator` and using
`Bump` with `std` collections. Note that, as `feature(allocator_api)` is
unstable and only in nightly Rust, Bumpalo’s matching `allocator_api` cargo
feature should be considered unstable, and will not follow the semver
conventions that the rest of the crate does.First, enable the `allocator_api` feature in your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
bumpalo = { version = "3", features = ["allocator_api"] }
```
Next, enable the `allocator_api` nightly Rust feature in your `src/lib.rs` or
`src/main.rs`:

Finally, use `std` collections with `Bump`, so that their internal heap
allocations are made within the given bump arena:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use bumpalo::Bump;
// Create a new bump arena.
let bump = Bump::new();
// Create a `Vec` whose elements are allocated within the bump arena.
let mut v = Vec::new_in(&bump);
v.push(0);
v.push(1);
v.push(2);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-the-allocator-api-on-stable-rust)Using the `Allocator` API on Stable Rust

You can enable the `allocator-api2` Cargo feature and `bumpalo` will use [the
 allocator-api2 crate](https://crates.io/crates/allocator-api2) to implement
the unstable nightly

`Allocator` API on stable Rust. This means that
`bumpalo::Bump` will be usable with any collection that is generic over
`allocator_api2::Allocator`.[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rust-version-msrv)Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV)

This crate is guaranteed to compile on stable Rust **1.71.1** and up. It might
compile with older versions but that may change in any new patch release.

We reserve the right to increment the MSRV on minor releases, however we will strive to only do it deliberately and for good reasons.

- A pointer type for bump allocation.
- [collections](https://docs.rs/collections/index.html)
- Collection types that allocate inside a `Bump`

- [vec](https://docs.rs/macro.vec.html)
- Creates a `Vec`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Alloc](https://docs.rs/struct.AllocErr.html)- Err
- The `AllocErr`error indicates an allocation failure that may be due to resource exhaustion or to something wrong when combining the given input arguments with this allocator.
- [Bump](https://docs.rs/struct.Bump.html)
- An arena to bump allocate into.
- [Chunk](https://docs.rs/struct.ChunkIter.html)- Iter

# log - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/log/^0.4/

## Expand description

A lightweight logging facade.

The `log` crate provides a single logging API that abstracts over the
actual logging implementation. Libraries can use the logging API provided
by this crate, and the consumer of those libraries can choose the logging
implementation that is most suitable for its use case.

If no logging implementation is selected, the facade falls back to a “noop” implementation that ignores all log messages. The overhead in this case is very small - just an integer load, comparison and jump.

A log request consists of a *target*, a *level*, and a *body*. A target is a
string which defaults to the module path of the location of the log request,
though that default may be overridden. Logger implementations typically use
the target to filter requests based on some user configuration.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The basic use of the log crate is through the five logging macros: [ error!](https://docs.rs/macro.error.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/macro.warn.html)

`warn!`[,](https://docs.rs/macro.info.html)

`info!`[and](https://docs.rs/macro.debug.html)

`debug!`[where](https://docs.rs/macro.trace.html)

`trace!``error!` represents the highest-priority log messages
and `trace!` the lowest. The log messages are filtered by configuring
the log level to exclude messages with a lower priority.
Each of these macros accept format strings similarly to [.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/macro.println.html)

`println!`Avoid writing expressions with side-effects in log statements. They may not be evaluated.

[§](https://docs.rs#in-libraries)In libraries

Libraries should link only to the `log` crate, and use the provided
macros to log whatever information will be useful to downstream consumers.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use log::{info, warn};
pub fn shave_the_yak(yak: &mut Yak) {
    info!(target: "yak_events", "Commencing yak shaving for {yak:?}");
    loop {
        match find_a_razor() {
            Ok(razor) => {
                info!("Razor located: {razor}");
                yak.shave(razor);
                break;
            }
            Err(err) => {
                warn!("Unable to locate a razor: {err}, retrying");
            }
        }
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#in-executables)In executables

Executables should choose a logging implementation and initialize it early in the runtime of the program. Logging implementations will typically include a function to do this. Any log messages generated before the implementation is initialized will be ignored.

The executable itself may use the `log` crate to log as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#warning)Warning

The logging system may only be initialized once.

[§](https://docs.rs#structured-logging)Structured logging

If you enable the `kv` feature you can associate structured values
with your log records. If we take the example from before, we can include
some additional context besides what’s in the formatted message:

```
use log::{info, warn};
pub fn shave_the_yak(yak: &mut Yak) {
    info!(target: "yak_events", yak:serde; "Commencing yak shaving");
    loop {
        match find_a_razor() {
            Ok(razor) => {
                info!(razor; "Razor located");
                yak.shave(razor);
                break;
            }
            Err(e) => {
                warn!(e:err; "Unable to locate a razor, retrying");
            }
        }
    }
}
```
See the [ kv](https://docs.rs/kv/index.html) module documentation for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#available-logging-implementations)Available logging implementations

In order to produce log output executables have to use a logger implementation compatible with the facade. There are many available implementations to choose from, here are some of the most popular ones:

- Simple minimal loggers:
- Complex configurable frameworks:
- Adaptors for other facilities:
- For WebAssembly binaries:
- For dynamic libraries:
- You may need to construct an FFI-safe wrapper over `log`to initialize in your libraries

- You may need to construct an FFI-safe wrapper over
- Utilities:

[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-a-logger)Implementing a Logger

Loggers implement the [ Log](https://docs.rs/trait.Log.html) trait. Here’s a very basic example that simply
logs all messages at the

[,](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Error`[or](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Warn`[levels to stdout:](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Info````
use log::{Record, Level, Metadata};
struct SimpleLogger;
impl log::Log for SimpleLogger {
    fn enabled(&self, metadata: &Metadata) -> bool {
        metadata.level() <= Level::Info
    }
    fn log(&self, record: &Record) {
        if self.enabled(record.metadata()) {
            println!("{} - {}", record.level(), record.args());
        }
    }
    fn flush(&self) {}
}
```
Loggers are installed by calling the [ set_logger](https://docs.rs/fn.set_logger.html) function. The maximum
log level also needs to be adjusted via the

[function. The logging facade uses this as an optimization to improve performance of log messages at levels that are disabled. It’s important to set it, as it defaults to](https://docs.rs/fn.set_max_level.html)

`set_max_level`[, so no log messages will ever be captured! In the case of our example logger, we’ll want to set the maximum log level to](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html)

`Off`[, since we ignore any](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html)

`Info`[or](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Debug`[level log messages. A logging implementation should provide a function that wraps a call to](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Trace`[and](https://docs.rs/fn.set_logger.html)

`set_logger`[, handling initialization of the logger:](https://docs.rs/fn.set_max_level.html)

`set_max_level````
use log::{SetLoggerError, LevelFilter};
static LOGGER: SimpleLogger = SimpleLogger;
pub fn init() -> Result<(), SetLoggerError> {
    log::set_logger(&LOGGER)
        .map(|()| log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info))
}
```
Implementations that adjust their configurations at runtime should take care to adjust the maximum log level as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#use-with-std)Use with `std`

`set_logger` requires you to provide a `&'static Log`, which can be hard to
obtain if your logger depends on some runtime configuration. The
`set_boxed_logger` function is available with the `std` Cargo feature. It is
identical to `set_logger` except that it takes a `Box<Log>` rather than a
`&'static Log`:

```
pub fn init() -> Result<(), SetLoggerError> {
    log::set_boxed_logger(Box::new(SimpleLogger))
        .map(|()| log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info))
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#compile-time-filters)Compile time filters

Log levels can be statically disabled at compile time by enabling one of these Cargo features:

- `max_level_off`
- `max_level_error`
- `max_level_warn`
- `max_level_info`
- `max_level_debug`
- `max_level_trace`

Log invocations at disabled levels will be skipped and will not even be present in the
resulting binary. These features control the value of the `STATIC_MAX_LEVEL` constant. The
logging macros check this value before logging a message. By default, no levels are disabled.

It is possible to override this level for release builds only with the following features:

- `release_max_level_off`
- `release_max_level_error`
- `release_max_level_warn`
- `release_max_level_info`
- `release_max_level_debug`
- `release_max_level_trace`

Libraries should avoid using the max level features because they’re global and can’t be changed once they’re set.

For example, a crate can disable trace level logs in debug builds and trace, debug, and info level logs in release builds with the following configuration:

```
[dependencies]
log = { version = "0.4", features = ["max_level_debug", "release_max_level_warn"] }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#crate-feature-flags)Crate Feature Flags

The following crate feature flags are available in addition to the filters. They are
configured in your `Cargo.toml`.

- `std`allows use of- `std`crate instead of the default- `core`. Enables using- `std::error`and- `set_boxed_logger`functionality.
- `serde`enables support for serialization and deserialization of- `Level`and- `LevelFilter`.

```
[dependencies]
log = { version = "0.4", features = ["std", "serde"] }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#version-compatibility)Version compatibility

The 0.3 and 0.4 versions of the `log` crate are almost entirely compatible. Log messages
made using `log` 0.3 will forward transparently to a logger implementation using `log` 0.4. Log
messages made using `log` 0.4 will forward to a logger implementation using `log` 0.3, but the
module path and file name information associated with the message will unfortunately be lost.

# proc_macro2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/^1.0/

## Expand description

A wrapper around the procedural macro API of the compiler’s [ proc_macro](https://doc.rust-lang.org/proc_macro/index.html)
crate. This library serves two purposes:

-
**Bring proc-macro-like functionality to other contexts like build.rs and main.rs.**Types from`proc_macro`are entirely specific to procedural macros and cannot ever exist in code outside of a procedural macro. Meanwhile`proc_macro2`types may exist anywhere including non-macro code. By developing foundational libraries like[syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn)and[quote](https://github.com/dtolnay/quote)against`proc_macro2`rather than`proc_macro`, the procedural macro ecosystem becomes easily applicable to many other use cases and we avoid reimplementing non-macro equivalents of those libraries.
-
**Make procedural macros unit testable.**As a consequence of being specific to procedural macros, nothing that uses`proc_macro`can be executed from a unit test. In order for helper libraries or components of a macro to be testable in isolation, they must be implemented using`proc_macro2`.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The skeleton of a typical procedural macro typically looks like this:

```
extern crate proc_macro;
#[proc_macro_derive(MyDerive)]
pub fn my_derive(input: proc_macro::TokenStream) -> proc_macro::TokenStream {
    let input = proc_macro2::TokenStream::from(input);
    let output: proc_macro2::TokenStream = {
        /* transform input */
    };
    proc_macro::TokenStream::from(output)
}
```
If parsing with [Syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn), you’ll use [ parse_macro_input!](https://docs.rs/syn/2.0/syn/macro.parse_macro_input.html) instead to
propagate parse errors correctly back to the compiler when parsing fails.

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-features)Unstable features

The default feature set of proc-macro2 tracks the most recent stable
compiler API. Functionality in `proc_macro` that is not yet stable is not
exposed by proc-macro2 by default.

To opt into the additional APIs available in the most recent nightly
compiler, the `procmacro2_semver_exempt` config flag must be passed to
rustc. We will polyfill those nightly-only APIs back to Rust 1.68.0. As
these are unstable APIs that track the nightly compiler, minor versions of
proc-macro2 may make breaking changes to them at any time.

`RUSTFLAGS='--cfg procmacro2_semver_exempt' cargo build`Note that this must not only be done for your crate, but for any crate that depends on your crate. This infectious nature is intentional, as it serves as a reminder that you are outside of the normal semver guarantees.

Semver exempt methods are marked as such in the proc-macro2 documentation.

[§](https://docs.rs#thread-safety)Thread-Safety

Most types in this crate are `!Sync` because the underlying compiler
types make use of thread-local memory, meaning they cannot be accessed from
a different thread.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [extra](https://docs.rs/extra/index.html)
- Items which do not have a correspondence to any API in the proc_macro crate, but are necessary to include in proc-macro2.
- [token_](https://docs.rs/token_stream/index.html)- stream
- Public implementation details for the `TokenStream`type, such as iterators.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Group](https://docs.rs/struct.Group.html)
- A delimited token stream.
- [Ident](https://docs.rs/struct.Ident.html)
- A word of Rust code, which may be a keyword or legal variable name.
- [LexError](https://docs.rs/struct.LexError.html)
- Error returned from `TokenStream::from_str`.
- [Line](https://docs.rs/struct.LineColumn.html)- Column - `span-locations`
- A line-column pair representing the start or end of a `Span`.
- [Literal](https://docs.rs/struct.Literal.html)
- A literal string (`"hello"`), byte string (`b"hello"`), character (`'a'`), byte character (`b'a'`), an integer or floating point number with or without a suffix (`1`,`1u8`,`2.3`,`2.3f32`).
- [Punct](https://docs.rs/struct.Punct.html)
- A `Punct`is a single punctuation character like`+`,`-`or`#`.
- [Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)
- A region of source code, along with macro expansion information.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/struct.TokenStream.html)- Stream
- An abstract stream of tokens, or more concretely a sequence of token trees.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Conversion](https://docs.rs/enum.ConversionErrorKind.html)- Error - Kind - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Error when retrieving a string literal’s unescaped value.
- [Delimiter](https://docs.rs/enum.Delimiter.html)
- Describes how a sequence of token trees is delimited.
- [Escape](https://docs.rs/enum.EscapeError.html)- Error - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Errors and warnings that can occur during string, char, and byte unescaping.
- [Spacing](https://docs.rs/enum.Spacing.html)
- Whether a `Punct`is followed immediately by another`Punct`or followed by another token or whitespace.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/enum.TokenTree.html)- Tree
- A single token or a delimited sequence of token trees (e.g. `[1, (), ..]`).

# quote - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quote/^1.0/

## Expand description

This crate provides the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for turning Rust syntax tree data
structures into tokens of source code.

Procedural macros in Rust receive a stream of tokens as input, execute arbitrary Rust code to determine how to manipulate those tokens, and produce a stream of tokens to hand back to the compiler to compile into the caller’s crate. Quasi-quoting is a solution to one piece of that — producing tokens to return to the compiler.

The idea of quasi-quoting is that we write *code* that we treat as *data*.
Within the `quote!` macro, we can write what looks like code to our text
editor or IDE. We get all the benefits of the editor’s brace matching,
syntax highlighting, indentation, and maybe autocompletion. But rather than
compiling that as code into the current crate, we can treat it as data, pass
it around, mutate it, and eventually hand it back to the compiler as tokens
to compile into the macro caller’s crate.

This crate is motivated by the procedural macro use case, but is a general-purpose Rust quasi-quoting library and is not specific to procedural macros.

```
[dependencies]
quote = "1.0"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The following quasi-quoted block of code is something you might find in [a](https://serde.rs/)
procedural macro having to do with data structure serialization. The `#var`
syntax performs interpolation of runtime variables into the quoted tokens.
Check out the documentation of the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for more detail about
the syntax. See also the

[macro which is important for implementing hygienic procedural macros.](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)

`quote_spanned!````
let tokens = quote! {
    struct SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        value: &'a #field_ty,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData<#item_ty>,
    }
    impl #generics serde::Serialize for SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
        where
            S: serde::Serializer,
        {
            #path(self.value, serializer)
        }
    }
    SerializeWith {
        value: #value,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData::<#item_ty>,
    }
};
```
[§](https://docs.rs#non-macro-code-generators)Non-macro code generators

When using `quote` in a build.rs or main.rs and writing the output out to a
file, consider having the code generator pass the tokens through
[prettyplease](https://github.com/dtolnay/prettyplease) before writing. This way if an error occurs in the generated
code it is convenient for a human to read and debug.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [format_](https://docs.rs/macro.format_ident.html)- ident
- Formatting macro for constructing `Ident`s.
- [quote](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html)
- The whole point.
- [quote_](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)- spanned
- Same as `quote!`, but applies a given span to all tokens originating within the macro invocation.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Ident](https://docs.rs/trait.IdentFragment.html)- Fragment
- Specialized formatting trait used by `format_ident!`.
- [ToTokens](https://docs.rs/trait.ToTokens.html)
- Types that can be interpolated inside a `quote!`invocation.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/trait.TokenStreamExt.html)- Stream - Ext
- TokenStream extension trait with methods for appending tokens.

---

# syn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/^2.0/

## Expand description

Syn is a parsing library for parsing a stream of Rust tokens into a syntax tree of Rust source code.

Currently this library is geared toward use in Rust procedural macros, but contains some APIs that may be useful more generally.

-
**Data structures**— Syn provides a complete syntax tree that can represent any valid Rust source code. The syntax tree is rooted at`syn::File``syn::Item``syn::Expr``syn::Type`
-
**Derives**— Of particular interest to derive macros is`syn::DeriveInput`
-
**Parsing**— Parsing in Syn is built around[parser functions](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)with the signature`fn(ParseStream) -> Result<T>`. Every syntax tree node defined by Syn is individually parsable and may be used as a building block for custom syntaxes, or you may dream up your own brand new syntax without involving any of our syntax tree types.
-
**Location information**— Every token parsed by Syn is associated with a`Span`that tracks line and column information back to the source of that token. These spans allow a procedural macro to display detailed error messages pointing to all the right places in the user’s code. There is an example of this below.
-
**Feature flags**— Functionality is aggressively feature gated so your procedural macros enable only what they need, and do not pay in compile time for all the rest.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-a-derive-macro)Example of a derive macro

The canonical derive macro using Syn looks like this. We write an ordinary
Rust function tagged with a `proc_macro_derive` attribute and the name of
the trait we are deriving. Any time that derive appears in the user’s code,
the Rust compiler passes their data structure as tokens into our macro. We
get to execute arbitrary Rust code to figure out what to do with those
tokens, then hand some tokens back to the compiler to compile into the
user’s crate.

```
[dependencies]
syn = "2.0"
quote = "1.0"
[lib]
proc-macro = true
```
```
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use quote::quote;
use syn::{parse_macro_input, DeriveInput};
#[proc_macro_derive(MyMacro)]
pub fn my_macro(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    // Parse the input tokens into a syntax tree
    let input = parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput);
    // Build the output, possibly using quasi-quotation
    let expanded = quote! {
        // ...
    };
    // Hand the output tokens back to the compiler
    TokenStream::from(expanded)
}
```
The [ heapsize](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/heapsize) example directory shows a complete working implementation
of a derive macro. The example derives a

`HeapSize` trait which computes an
estimate of the amount of heap memory owned by a value.```
pub trait HeapSize {
    /// Total number of bytes of heap memory owned by `self`.
    fn heap_size_of_children(&self) -> usize;
}
```
The derive macro allows users to write `#[derive(HeapSize)]` on data
structures in their program.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Demo<'a, T: ?Sized> {
    a: Box<T>,
    b: u8,
    c: &'a str,
    d: String,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#spans-and-error-reporting)Spans and error reporting

The token-based procedural macro API provides great control over where the
compiler’s error messages are displayed in user code. Consider the error the
user sees if one of their field types does not implement `HeapSize`.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Broken {
    ok: String,
    bad: std::thread::Thread,
}
```
By tracking span information all the way through the expansion of a
procedural macro as shown in the `heapsize` example, token-based macros in
Syn are able to trigger errors that directly pinpoint the source of the
problem.

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `std::thread::Thread: HeapSize` is not satisfied
 --> src/main.rs:7:5
  |
7 |     bad: std::thread::Thread,
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the trait `HeapSize` is not implemented for `Thread`
```
[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-a-custom-syntax)Parsing a custom syntax

The [ lazy-static](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/lazy-static) example directory shows the implementation of a

`functionlike!(...)` procedural macro in which the input tokens are parsed
using Syn’s parsing API.The example reimplements the popular `lazy_static` crate from crates.io as a
procedural macro.

```
lazy_static! {
    static ref USERNAME: Regex = Regex::new("^[a-z0-9_-]{3,16}$").unwrap();
}
```
The implementation shows how to trigger custom warnings and error messages on the macro input.

```
warning: come on, pick a more creative name
  --> src/main.rs:10:16
   |
10 |     static ref FOO: String = "lazy_static".to_owned();
   |                ^^^
```
[§](https://docs.rs#testing)Testing

When testing macros, we often care not just that the macro can be used
successfully but also that when the macro is provided with invalid input it
produces maximally helpful error messages. Consider using the [ trybuild](https://github.com/dtolnay/trybuild)
crate to write tests for errors that are emitted by your macro or errors
detected by the Rust compiler in the expanded code following misuse of the
macro. Such tests help avoid regressions from later refactors that
mistakenly make an error no longer trigger or be less helpful than it used
to be.

[§](https://docs.rs#debugging)Debugging

When developing a procedural macro it can be helpful to look at what the
generated code looks like. Use `cargo rustc -- -Zunstable-options -Zunpretty=expanded` or the [ cargo expand](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand) subcommand.

To show the expanded code for some crate that uses your procedural macro,
run `cargo expand` from that crate. To show the expanded code for one of
your own test cases, run `cargo expand --test the_test_case` where the last
argument is the name of the test file without the `.rs` extension.

This write-up by Brandon W Maister discusses debugging in more detail:
[Debugging Rust’s new Custom Derive system](https://quodlibetor.github.io/posts/debugging-rusts-new-custom-derive-system/).

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

Syn puts a lot of functionality behind optional features in order to optimize compile time for the most common use cases. The following features are available.

- `derive`- *(enabled by default)*— Data structures for representing the possible input to a derive macro, including structs and enums and types.
- `full`
- `parsing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to parse input tokens into a syntax tree node of a chosen type.
- `printing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to print a syntax tree node as tokens of Rust source code.
- `visit`
- `visit-mut`
- `fold`
- `clone-impls`- *(enabled by default)*— Clone impls for all syntax tree types.
- `extra-traits`
- `proc-macro`- *(enabled by default)*— Runtime dependency on the dynamic library libproc_macro from rustc toolchain.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [buffer](https://docs.rs/buffer/index.html)- `parsing`
- A stably addressed token buffer supporting efficient traversal based on a cheaply copyable cursor.
- [ext](https://docs.rs/ext/index.html)
- Extension traits to provide parsing methods on foreign types.
- [fold](https://docs.rs/fold/index.html)- `fold`
- Syntax tree traversal to transform the nodes of an owned syntax tree.
- [meta](https://docs.rs/meta/index.html)- `parsing`and (- `derive`or- `full`)
- Facility for interpreting structured content inside of an `Attribute`.
- [parse](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)- `parsing`
- Parsing interface for parsing a token stream into a syntax tree node.
- [punctuated](https://docs.rs/punctuated/index.html)
- A punctuated sequence of syntax tree nodes separated by punctuation.
- [spanned](https://docs.rs/spanned/index.html)- `parsing`and- `printing`
- A trait that can provide the `Span`of the complete contents of a syntax tree node.
- [token](https://docs.rs/token/index.html)
- Tokens representing Rust punctuation, keywords, and delimiters.
- [visit](https://docs.rs/visit/index.html)- `visit`
- Syntax tree traversal to walk a shared borrow of a syntax tree.
- [visit_](https://docs.rs/visit_mut/index.html)- mut - `visit-mut`
- Syntax tree traversal to mutate an exclusive borrow of a syntax tree in place.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [Token](https://docs.rs/macro.Token.html)
- A type-macro that expands to the name of the Rust type representation of a given token.
- [braced](https://docs.rs/macro.braced.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of curly braces and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [bracketed](https://docs.rs/macro.bracketed.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of square brackets and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_keyword.html)- keyword
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a given identifier as if it were a keyword.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_punctuation.html)- punctuation
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a multi-character symbol as if it were a punctuation token.
- [parenthesized](https://docs.rs/macro.parenthesized.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of parentheses and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_macro_input.html)- macro_ - input - `parsing`and- `proc-macro`
- Parse the input TokenStream of a macro, triggering a compile error if the tokens fail to parse.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote.html)- quote - `parsing`and- `printing`
- Quasi-quotation macro that accepts input like the `quote!`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote_spanned.html)- quote_ - spanned - `parsing`and- `printing`
- This macro is `parse_quote!``quote_spanned!`

- Unnamed fields of a tuple struct or tuple variant such as `Some(T)`.
- [File](https://docs.rs/struct.File.html)- `full`
- A complete file of Rust source code.
- [Foreign](https://docs.rs/struct.ForeignItemFn.html)- Item - Fn - `full`
- A foreign function in an `extern`block.
- [Foreign](https://docs.rs/struct.ForeignItemMacro.html)- Item - Macro - `full`
- A macro invocation within an extern block.
- [Foreign](https://docs.rs/struct.ForeignItemStatic.html)- Item - Static - `full`
- A foreign static item in an `extern`block:`static ext: u8`.
- [Foreign](https://docs.rs/struct.ForeignItemType.html)- Item - Type - `full`
- A foreign type in an `extern`block:`type void`.
- [Generics](https://docs.rs/struct.Generics.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- Lifetimes and type parameters attached to a declaration of a function, enum, trait, etc.
- [Ident](https://docs.rs/struct.Ident.html)
- A word of Rust code, which may be a keyword or legal variable name.
- [Impl](https://docs.rs/struct.ImplGenerics.html)- Generics - `printing`and (- `derive`or- `full`)
- Returned by `Generics::split_for_impl`.
- [Impl](https://docs.rs/struct.ImplItemConst.html)- Item - Const - `full`
- An associated constant within an impl block.
- [Impl](https://docs.rs/struct.ImplItemFn.html)- Item - Fn - `full`
- An associated function within an impl block.
- [Impl](https://docs.rs/struct.ImplItemMacro.html)- Item - Macro - `full`
- A macro invocation within an impl block.
- [Impl](https://docs.rs/struct.ImplItemType.html)- Item - Type - `full`
- An associated type within an impl block.
- [Index](https://docs.rs/struct.Index.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- The index of an unnamed tuple struct field.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemConst.html)- Const - `full`
- A constant item: `const MAX: u16 = 65535`.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemEnum.html)- Enum - `full`
- An enum definition: `enum Foo<A, B> { A(A), B(B) }`.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemExternCrate.html)- Extern - Crate - `full`
- An `extern crate`item:`extern crate serde`.
- [ItemFn](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemFn.html)- `full`
- A free-standing function: `fn process(n: usize) -> Result<()> { ... }`.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemForeignMod.html)- Foreign - Mod - `full`
- A block of foreign items: `extern "C" { ... }`.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemImpl.html)- Impl - `full`
- An impl block providing trait or associated items: `impl<A> Trait for Data<A> { ... }`.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemMacro.html)- Macro - `full`
- A macro invocation, which includes `macro_rules!`definitions.
- [ItemMod](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemMod.html)- `full`
- A module or module declaration: `mod m`or`mod m { ... }`.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemStatic.html)- Static - `full`
- A static item: `static BIKE: Shed = Shed(42)`.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemStruct.html)- Struct - `full`
- A struct definition: `struct Foo<A> { x: A }`.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemTrait.html)- Trait - `full`
- A trait definition: `pub trait Iterator { ... }`.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemTraitAlias.html)- Trait - Alias - `full`
- A trait alias: `pub trait SharableIterator = Iterator + Sync`.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemType.html)- Type - `full`
- A type alias: `type Result<T> = core::result::Result<T, MyError>`.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemUnion.html)- Union - `full`
- A union definition: `union Foo<A, B> { x: A, y: B }`.
- [ItemUse](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemUse.html)- `full`
- A use declaration: `use alloc::collections::HashMap`.
- [Label](https://docs.rs/struct.Label.html)- `full`
- A lifetime labeling a `for`,`while`, or`loop`.
- [Lifetime](https://docs.rs/struct.Lifetime.html)
- A Rust lifetime: `'a`.
- [Lifetime](https://docs.rs/struct.LifetimeParam.html)- Param - `derive`or- `full`
- A lifetime definition: `'a: 'b + 'c + 'd`.
- [LitBool](https://docs.rs/struct.LitBool.html)
- A boolean literal: `true`or`false`.
- [LitByte](https://docs.rs/struct.LitByte.html)
- A byte literal: `b'f'`.
- [LitByte](https://docs.rs/struct.LitByteStr.html)- Str
- A byte string literal: `b"foo"`.
- [LitCStr](https://docs.rs/struct.LitCStr.html)
- A nul-terminated C-string literal: `c"foo"`.
- [LitChar](https://docs.rs/struct.LitChar.html)
- A character literal: `'a'`.
- [LitFloat](https://docs.rs/struct.LitFloat.html)
- A floating point literal: `1f64`or`1.0e10f64`.
- [LitInt](https://docs.rs/struct.LitInt.html)
- An integer literal: `1`or`1u16`.
- [LitStr](https://docs.rs/struct.LitStr.html)
- A UTF-8 string literal: `"foo"`.
- [Local](https://docs.rs/struct.Local.html)- `full`
- A local `let`binding:`let x: u64 = s.parse()?;`.

- A range expression: `1..2`,`1..`,`..2`,`1..=2`,`..=2`.
- [PatReference](https://docs.rs/struct.PatReference.html)- `full`
- A reference pattern: `&mut var`.

# wasm_bindgen_backend - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wasm-bindgen-backend/latest/target-redirect/wasm_bindgen_backend/

## Expand description

A common backend for bindgen crates.

This (internal) crate provides functionality common to multiple bindgen dependency crates. There are 4 main things exported from this crate:

-
Provides the ability to attempt conversion from an AST struct into a TokenStream
-
A struct used to provide diagnostic responses for failures of said tokenization
-
Abstract Syntax Tree types used to represent a Rust program, with the necessary metadata to generate bindings for it
-
Common utilities for manipulating parsed types from syn

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [ast](https://docs.rs/ast/index.html)
- A representation of the Abstract Syntax Tree of a Rust program, with all the added metadata necessary to generate Wasm bindings for it.
- [util](https://docs.rs/util/index.html)
- Common utility function for manipulating syn types and handling parsed values

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [bail_](https://docs.rs/macro.bail_span.html)- span
- Immediately fail and return an Err, with the arguments passed to err_span!
- [err_](https://docs.rs/macro.err_span.html)- span
- Provide a Diagnostic with the given span and message

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Diagnostic](https://docs.rs/struct.Diagnostic.html)
- A struct representing a diagnostic to emit to the end-user as an error.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [TryTo](https://docs.rs/trait.TryToTokens.html)- Tokens
- A trait for converting AST structs into Tokens and adding them to a TokenStream, or providing a diagnostic if conversion fails.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# reifydb_profiler - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/reifydb-profiler/0.7.0/reifydb_profiler/

## Expand description

Always-on profiler primitives. Builds on `tracing` to capture per-scope span records without allocating on the hot
path. `ProfilerLayer` is a `tracing_subscriber::Layer` that intercepts spans matching a curated set of
`ProfilerCategory` prefixes, extracts numeric fields through reusable thread-local visitors, and appends a
fixed-size `MinimalSpanRecord` to scope-local state. `ProfilerScope::start` opens a scope; `ScopeHandle::finish`
drains the accumulated records, builds a `ProfilerSummary` for the caller, and hands the batch to a `ProfilerSink`
for downstream delivery (in production this is `sub-profiler`’s EventBus bridge).

This crate stays free of any metric or IoC dependency so the layer can be embedded in tests with a `NoopSink` and
so the rest of the workspace can use the data model without pulling in the subsystem.

# reifydb_column - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/reifydb-column/0.7.0/reifydb_column/

## Expand description

Columnar storage engine: the immutable, on-disk representation of materialized columns plus the read-time machinery (compute kernels, predicates, scans, selection vectors, snapshots) the engine uses to query them. This crate owns the bucket layout and the per-column compression and encoding schemes.

Read paths come in here, get a column reader, and stream values through compute kernels that operate directly on the encoded bytes where possible - decoding only when a kernel cannot run on the encoded form. The snapshot type is what the subscription tier hands out to consumers so they can iterate over a stable view of the column without racing against ongoing writes.

Invariant: a column’s encoded bytes plus its stats and bitmap are produced together and never updated piecewise. Tearing those apart - rewriting just the values, just the bitmap, or just the stats - means readers can observe a column whose statistics no longer describe its contents, which silently corrupts every kernel that reads stats to skip work.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [bucket](https://docs.rs/bucket/index.html)
- [compress](https://docs.rs/compress/index.html)
- [compute](https://docs.rs/compute/index.html)
- Compute kernels that operate on encoded columns. Compare, take, slice, filter, sum, search-sorted, min/max - the primitives the engine VM dispatches to when it executes the per-instruction work of a query. Kernels prefer to run directly on the encoded bytes (canonical layout, dictionary indices, run-length runs) and only decode when they cannot.
- [encoding](https://docs.rs/encoding/index.html)
- Per-column encoding implementations. Canonical is the dense unencoded layout; the compressed family covers all-none, bit-packed, constant, delta, delta-RLE, dictionary, frame-of-reference, run-length, and sparse forms. Each encoding produces and consumes the same encoded-bytes contract so compute kernels can be written once and work across encodings.
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- [predicate](https://docs.rs/predicate/index.html)
- [reader](https://docs.rs/reader/index.html)
- [scan](https://docs.rs/scan/index.html)
- [selection](https://docs.rs/selection/index.html)
- [snapshot](https://docs.rs/snapshot/index.html)

---

# transmux - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/transmux/0.6.0/transmux/

## Expand description

`transmux` — MPEG-2 TS → CMAF/fMP4 container remux (ISO/IEC 14496-12:2015).

A **samples-in** container multiplexer: the caller supplies demuxed *coded*
access units + codec config, and `transmux` produces CMAF initialization and
media segments plus HLS playlists. It parses codec config/parameter headers
(SPS/PPS/VPS, AAC ASC, AC-3/E-AC-3 syncframe BSI) only to build the container
boxes and derive metadata — it never encodes or decodes media; coded samples
pass through opaque. `no_std` + `alloc`.

See the crate README for the full **feature matrix** (implemented boxes and
codecs plus planned coverage). Key entry points: [ build_init_segment](https://docs.rs/pipeline/fn.build_init_segment.html) and

[(batch),](https://docs.rs/pipeline/fn.build_media_segment.html)

`build_media_segment`[(streaming),](https://docs.rs/segmenter/struct.Segmenter.html)

`Segmenter`[with](https://docs.rs/nalu_types/struct.AvcSps.html#method.decode)

`AvcSps::decode`[(codec metadata), and the HLS playlist builders.](https://docs.rs/nalu_types/struct.AvcSps.html#method.rfc6381)

`AvcSps::rfc6381`This crate root also exposes the low-level ISOBMFF framing it is built on:
[ BoxHeader](https://docs.rs/box_types/struct.BoxHeader.html) (optional 64-bit

`largesize` / `uuid` extended type),
[(](https://docs.rs/box_types/struct.FullBoxHeader.html)

`FullBoxHeader``version` + `flags`), and a size-driven box walker
([) that skips unknown box types by advancing by](https://docs.rs/box_types/struct.BoxIter.html)

`BoxIter``size`.[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick start

```
use transmux::{box_iter, parse_box, BoxHeader, BoxType};
use broadcast_common::Parse;
// Parse a simple ftyp box header.
let bytes = [0, 0, 0, 12, b'f', b't', b'y', b'p', 0, 0, 0, 0];
let header = BoxHeader::parse(&bytes).unwrap();
assert_eq!(header.box_type.to_string(), "ftyp");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#spec-citations)Spec citations

- **Box / FullBox**: ISO/IEC 14496-12:2015 §4.2 (fulltext L1254–L1304).
- **Box order**: §6.2.3 (recommendations; only- `ftyp`before variable-length and- `moof`sequence_number are mandatory).
- **Skip-unknown rule**: §4.2 L1294 — unknown type → ignore + skip via size.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

| Feature | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `std` | yes | `std::error::Error`impls |
| `serde` | yes | `serde::Serialize`for box types |

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use aac_asc::`- [build_adts_header](https://docs.rs/aac_asc/fn.build_adts_header.html);
- `pub use aac_asc::`- [parse_adts_header](https://docs.rs/aac_asc/fn.parse_adts_header.html);
- `pub use aac_asc::`- [AdtsHeader](https://docs.rs/aac_asc/struct.AdtsHeader.html);
- `pub use aac_asc::`- [AudioObjectType](https://docs.rs/aac_asc/enum.AudioObjectType.html);
- `pub use aac_asc::`- [AudioSpecificConfig](https://docs.rs/aac_asc/struct.AudioSpecificConfig.html);
- `pub use aac_asc::`- [ChannelConfiguration](https://docs.rs/aac_asc/enum.ChannelConfiguration.html);
- `pub use aac_asc::`- [HeAacSignaling](https://docs.rs/aac_asc/struct.HeAacSignaling.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [aac_asc](https://docs.rs/aac_asc/index.html)
- AAC `AudioSpecificConfig`(ASC) — ISO/IEC 14496-3:2001 §1.6.2.1 Table 1.8.
- [ac3](https://docs.rs/ac3/index.html)
- AC-3 and Enhanced AC-3 in ISOBMFF — ETSI TS 102 366 Annex F.
- [ac4](https://docs.rs/ac4/index.html)
- AC-4 in ISOBMFF — `ac-4`AudioSampleEntry +`dac4`config box.
- [annexb](https://docs.rs/annexb/index.html)
- Annex B ↔ length-prefixed NAL conversion — ITU-T H.264 Annex B / ISO/IEC 14496-15 §5.3.4.
- [av1](https://docs.rs/av1/index.html)
- AV1 in ISOBMFF — `av01`VisualSampleEntry +`av1C`config box.
- [avc_](https://docs.rs/avc_config/index.html)- config
- AVC decoder configuration record (`avcC`) — ISO/IEC 14496-15:2017 §5.3.3.
- [bitreader](https://docs.rs/bitreader/index.html)
- Exp-Golomb bit reader over an RBSP byte stream.
- [box_](https://docs.rs/box_types/index.html)- types
- ISOBMFF Box/FullBox layer — ISO/IEC 14496-12:2015 §4.2.
- [cenc](https://docs.rs/cenc/index.html)
- Common Encryption boxes — ISO/IEC 23001-7 (CENC) + ISO/IEC 14496-12:2015 §8.12.
- [dts](https://docs.rs/dts/index.html)
- DTS audio in ISOBMFF — `dtsc`/`dtsh`/`dtsl`/`dtse`AudioSampleEntry +`ddts`config box.
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Error type returned by every parser and builder in this crate.
- [flac](https://docs.rs/flac/index.html)
- FLAC in ISOBMFF — `fLaC`AudioSampleEntry +`dfLa`config box.
- [hevc_](https://docs.rs/hevc_config/index.html)- config
- HEVC decoder configuration record (`hvcC`) — ISO/IEC 14496-15:2017 §8.3.3.
- [hls](https://docs.rs/hls/index.html)
- HLS playlist generation — RFC 8216.
- [init_](https://docs.rs/init_segment/index.html)- segment
- Typed init-segment (moov) box tree — ISO/IEC 14496-12:2015 §8.2–8.7.
- [movie_](https://docs.rs/movie_fragment/index.html)- fragment
- Movie Fragment boxes - ISO/IEC 14496-12:2015 Â§8.8.
- [mp4esds](https://docs.rs/mp4esds/index.html)
- MPEG-4 elementary-stream descriptor chain (`esds`box) — ISO/IEC 14496-1:2010 §7.2.6 / ISO/IEC 14496-14:2003 §5.6.
- [mpegh](https://docs.rs/mpegh/index.html)
- MPEG-H 3D Audio in ISOBMFF — `mha1`/`mhm1`+`mhaC`(ISO/IEC 23008-3 §20).
- [nalu_](https://docs.rs/nalu_types/index.html)- types
- NAL unit byte-slice newtypes and typed arrays for AVC/HEVC decoder config records.
- [opus](https://docs.rs/opus/index.html)
- Opus in ISOBMFF — `Opus`AudioSampleEntry +`dOps`config box.
- [pipeline](https://docs.rs/pipeline/index.html)
- TS → CMAF/fMP4 remux pipeline — the muxer above the box builders.
- [sample_](https://docs.rs/sample_entries/index.html)- entries
- AVC/HEVC sample entries and their config boxes — ISO/IEC 14496-15:2017 §5.4, §8.4.
- [sample_](https://docs.rs/sample_groups/index.html)- groups
- ProducerReferenceTimeBox, SampleGroupDescriptionBox, SampleToGroupBox, and SubSampleInformationBox — ISO/IEC 14496-12:2015 §8.16.5, §8.9.2, §8.9.3, §8.7.7.
- [segmenter](https://docs.rs/segmenter/index.html)
- Stateful CMAF segmenter — a streaming wrapper over `build_init_segment``build_media_segment`
- [segments](https://docs.rs/segments/index.html)
- Segment-level ISOBMFF boxes — ISO/IEC 14496-12:2015.
- [sps](https://docs.rs/sps/index.html)
- H.264 / H.265 sequence parameter set (SPS) decode.
- [subtitle_](https://docs.rs/subtitle_entries/index.html)- entries
- ISO/IEC 14496-30 subtitle sample entries — `stpp`(TTML/IMSC) and`wvtt`(WebVTT).
- [timing](https://docs.rs/timing/index.html)
- Sample-timing and segment-index boxes — ISO/IEC 14496-12:2015 §8.6/§8.16.
- [visual_](https://docs.rs/visual_ext/index.html)- ext
- Visual sample-entry extension boxes — ISO/IEC 14496-12:2015 §12.1.4–5.
- [vp9](https://docs.rs/vp9/index.html)
- VP9 in ISOBMFF — `vp09`VisualSampleEntry +`vpcC`config box.

# aviutl2_eframe - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/aviutl2-eframe/0.35.0/aviutl2_eframe/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#aviutl2-eframe)aviutl2-eframe

AviUtl2の汎用プラグインでegui/eframeを扱うためのライブラリ。

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

- `default_fonts`（デフォルト）：eguiのデフォルトフォントを埋め込むかどうか。 無効にするとeguiにて使われている記号が表示されなくなる可能性があるので、通常は有効にしておくことを推奨します。
- `transparent_keyboard_input`（デフォルト）：eguiがキーボード入力を要求していないときにAviUtl2にキーボードイベントを透過させるかどうか。

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

aviutl2-rsをGitリポジトリで依存として指定する場合は`[patch]`セクションを使用してください。
もし`aviutl2 = { git = "..." }`のように直接指定した場合、`aviutl2-eframe`クレートから
参照する`aviutl2`クレートと依存関係が分裂してしまい、特に[ aviutl2_visuals](https://docs.rs/fn.aviutl2_visuals.html)関数などで問題が発生します。

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [AviUtl2](https://docs.rs/struct.AviUtl2EframeHandle.html)- Eframe - Handle
- aviutl2-eframeでウィンドウ内から呼び出される関数のハンドル。
- [Eframe](https://docs.rs/struct.EframeWindow.html)- Window
- eframeのウィンドウを表す構造体。
- [Eframe](https://docs.rs/struct.EframeWindowHandle.html)- Window - Handle
- EframeWindowのウィンドウハンドル。

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [aviutl2_](https://docs.rs/fn.aviutl2_fonts.html)- fonts
- AviUtl2で指定されているフォントからeguiのFontDefinitionsを作成する。
- [aviutl2_](https://docs.rs/fn.aviutl2_visuals.html)- visuals
- AviUtl2のテーマに基づいたeguiのVisualsを取得する。

# aviutl2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/aviutl2/0.35.0/aviutl2/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#aviutl2-rs)aviutl2-rs

AviUtl2 SDKのRustラッパー。 このクレートは、AviUtl2のプラグインをRustらしく開発できるようにすることを目的としています。

[§](https://docs.rs#%E3%83%A2%E3%82%B8%E3%83%A5%E3%83%BC%E3%83%AB)モジュール

- `input`
- `output`
- `filter`
- `module`
- `generic`
- `logger`
- `config`
- `cache`
- `common`
- `utils`

詳細は各モジュールのドキュメントを参照してください。

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

- `input`（デフォルト）：入力プラグイン機能を有効にします。
- `output`（デフォルト）：出力プラグイン機能を有効にします。
- `filter`（デフォルト）：フィルタプラグイン機能を有効にします。
- `module`（デフォルト）：スクリプトモジュールプラグイン機能を有効にします。
- `generic`（デフォルト）：汎用プラグイン機能を有効にします。
- `wrap_log`（デフォルト）：ログ出力時に自動で改行を追加します。
- `aviutl2-alias`：（デフォルト）- `aviutl2_alias`クレートを依存関係として追加し、いくつかの関数を追加します。
- `image`：- `image`クレートを使用して画像の読み書きをサポートします。
- `serde`：- `serde`を使用してプロジェクトファイルへのデータの保存と読み込みをサポートします。

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

[§](https://docs.rs#%E5%86%85%E9%83%A8%E3%82%A2%E3%82%A4%E3%83%86%E3%83%A0%E3%81%AB%E3%81%A4%E3%81%84%E3%81%A6)内部アイテムについて

このクレートにて、`__`で始まる名前のモジュールや関数やマクロは内部実装用です。
マクロなどを通じて利用されることを意図しており、直接使用した場合の互換性は保証されません。
これらのアイテムはsemverの保証対象外であり、予告なく変更または削除される可能性があります。

# crossterm_keybind - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crossterm-keybind/0.4.3/crossterm_keybind/

## Expand description

This crate help you build tui with keybings config in an easy way. When building a tui application, we need address following topics.

- `Define a set of keybing for some events`
- `Capture one/some key bindings and perform one the event`
- `Display a prompt of a key bindings`
- `Provide a config file and let user to change all or part of it`

These topics can be abstract these into [ KeyBindTrait](https://docs.rs/trait.KeyBindTrait.html), and the key binding serialize and deserialize
to a config file are solved in this crate.

There still are a lot of trivial works, ahead you and your great ideal to build tui application.
This crate also provides derive macro [KeyBind](https://docs.rs/crossterm-keybind-derive/latest/crossterm_keybind_derive/derive.KeyBind.html)
to generate the the keyconfig in a supper easy way, you can have a toml key config for your
events and allow user to patch part of it.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [struct_patch](https://docs.rs/struct-patch/0.12.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/struct_patch/index.html);
- `pub use`- [toml](https://docs.rs/toml/1.1.2+spec-1.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/toml/index.html);
- `pub use`- [toml_example](https://docs.rs/toml-example/0.16.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/toml_example/index.html);
- `pub use`- [log](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.33/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/index.html);
- `pub use`- [serde](https://docs.rs/serde/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde/index.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [event](https://docs.rs/event/index.html)
- A module to read events.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [KeyBinding](https://docs.rs/struct.KeyBinding.html)
- [KeyBindings](https://docs.rs/struct.KeyBindings.html)
- KeyBindings struct for key bind configure

# wasm-bindgen-backend 0.2.104 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wasm-bindgen-backend/0.2.104

A common backend for bindgen crates.

This (internal) crate provides functionality common to multiple bindgen dependency crates. There are 4 main things exported from this crate:

-
Provides the ability to attempt conversion from an AST struct into a TokenStream
-
A struct used to provide diagnostic responses for failures of said tokenization
-
Abstract Syntax Tree types used to represent a Rust program, with the necessary metadata to generate bindings for it
-
Common utilities for manipulating parsed types from syn

# wasm_bindgen_backend - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wasm-bindgen-backend/0.2.104/target-redirect/wasm_bindgen_backend/

## Expand description

A common backend for bindgen crates.

This (internal) crate provides functionality common to multiple bindgen dependency crates. There are 4 main things exported from this crate:

-
Provides the ability to attempt conversion from an AST struct into a TokenStream
-
A struct used to provide diagnostic responses for failures of said tokenization
-
Abstract Syntax Tree types used to represent a Rust program, with the necessary metadata to generate bindings for it
-
Common utilities for manipulating parsed types from syn

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [ast](https://docs.rs/ast/index.html)
- A representation of the Abstract Syntax Tree of a Rust program, with all the added metadata necessary to generate Wasm bindings for it.
- [util](https://docs.rs/util/index.html)
- Common utility function for manipulating syn types and handling parsed values

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [bail_](https://docs.rs/macro.bail_span.html)- span
- Immediately fail and return an Err, with the arguments passed to err_span!
- [err_](https://docs.rs/macro.err_span.html)- span
- Provide a Diagnostic with the given span and message

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Diagnostic](https://docs.rs/struct.Diagnostic.html)
- A struct representing a diagnostic to emit to the end-user as an error.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [TryTo](https://docs.rs/trait.TryToTokens.html)- Tokens
- A trait for converting AST structs into Tokens and adding them to a TokenStream, or providing a diagnostic if conversion fails.

# wasm_bindgen_backend::ast - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen-backend/0.2.104/wasm_bindgen_backend/ast/index.html

## Expand description

A representation of the Abstract Syntax Tree of a Rust program, with all the added metadata necessary to generate Wasm bindings for it.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Enum](https://docs.rs/struct.Enum.html)
- The metadata for an Enum
- [Export](https://docs.rs/struct.Export.html)
- A rust to js interface. Allows interaction with rust objects/functions from javascript.
- [Function](https://docs.rs/struct.Function.html)
- Information about a function being imported or exported
- [Function](https://docs.rs/struct.FunctionArgumentData.html)- Argument - Data
- Information about a function’s argument
- [Function](https://docs.rs/struct.FunctionReturnData.html)- Return - Data
- Information about a function’s return
- [Import](https://docs.rs/struct.Import.html)
- Things imported from a JS module (in an `extern`block)
- [Import](https://docs.rs/struct.ImportFunction.html)- Function
- A function being imported from JS
- [Import](https://docs.rs/struct.ImportStatic.html)- Static
- The type of a static being imported
- [Import](https://docs.rs/struct.ImportString.html)- String
- The type of a static string being imported
- [Import](https://docs.rs/struct.ImportType.html)- Type
- The metadata for a type being imported
- [Link](https://docs.rs/struct.LinkToModule.html)- ToModule
- An abstract syntax tree representing a link to a module in Rust. In contrast to Program, LinkToModule must expand to an expression. linked_modules of the inner Program must contain exactly one element whose link is produced by the expression.
- [Operation](https://docs.rs/struct.Operation.html)
- The operation performed by a class method
- [Program](https://docs.rs/struct.Program.html)
- An abstract syntax tree representing a rust program. Contains extra information for joining up this rust code with javascript.
- [String](https://docs.rs/struct.StringEnum.html)- Enum
- The metadata for a String Enum
- [Struct](https://docs.rs/struct.Struct.html)
- Information about a Struct being exported
- [Struct](https://docs.rs/struct.StructField.html)- Field
- The field of a struct
- [Variant](https://docs.rs/struct.Variant.html)
- The variant of an enum

- Unused, the type of an argument to / return from a function
- [Type](https://docs.rs/enum.TypeLocation.html)- Location
- Unused, the location of a type for a function argument (import/export, argument/ret)

# wasm_bindgen_backend::util - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen-backend/0.2.104/wasm_bindgen_backend/util/index.html

## Expand description

Common utility function for manipulating syn types and handling parsed values

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Short](https://docs.rs/struct.ShortHash.html)- Hash
- Small utility used when generating symbol names.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [ident_](https://docs.rs/fn.ident_ty.html)- ty
- Create a path type with a single segment from a given Identifier
- [leading_](https://docs.rs/fn.leading_colon_path_ty.html)- colon_ - path_ - ty
- Create a global path type from the given segments. For example an iterator
yielding the idents `[foo, bar, baz]`will result in the path type`::foo::bar::baz`.
- [raw_](https://docs.rs/fn.raw_ident.html)- ident
- Create an `Ident`without checking to see if it conflicts with a Rust keyword.
- [rust_](https://docs.rs/fn.rust_ident.html)- ident
- Create an `Ident`, possibly mangling it if it conflicts with a Rust keyword.
- [simple_](https://docs.rs/fn.simple_path_ty.html)- path_ - ty
- Create a path type from the given segments. For example an iterator yielding
the idents `[foo, bar, baz]`will result in the path type`foo::bar::baz`.
- [wrap_](https://docs.rs/fn.wrap_import_function.html)- import_ - function
- Convert an ImportFunction into the more generic Import type, wrapping the provided function
